From a music theory standpoint, this is one of Paul McCartney’s most celebrated uses of modal mixture and baroque-pop harmony. The song opens in the key of B major with the signature staccato piano chords. Instead of moving diatonically to the standard major dominant (F# major) or the relative minor (G#m), McCartney immediately shifts on the second chord to an **F# minor** (the minor fifth / v chord). 

This abrupt drop into the minor dominant right at the start gives the opening line ("Penny Lane, there is a barber showing photographs...") its distinctive bittersweet, slightly nostalgic tonal color before it continues modulating through the verse. Therefore, "Penny Lane" fits the description of starting with a direct jump from the tonic to the minor fifth chord.

In Western tonal harmony—and specifically early 1960s pop, rock, and British Invasion songwriting—minor-key songs almost **never** stayed strictly in natural minor/Aeolian.
